questions.prompt: What makes an org officially count as "Large Data Volumes," per this course?
options: An elastic, behavior-based threshold — commonly framed around tens of millions of records in an object, hundreds of GB of storage, or tens of thousands of users — rather than one fixed record count
Exactly 1,000,000 records in any single object, with no exceptions
More than 50 custom objects defined in the org
Any org that has been live in production for more than five years
questions.explain: Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 are explicit that Salesforce frames LDV as an elastic, imprecise term oriented around several rough dimensions used together, not a single fixed record count that automatically applies once crossed.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B treats LDV as a precise numeric trigger, but the course explicitly rejects that framing — a well-designed org can comfortably exceed a million records with no LDV symptoms, while a poorly-designed, skewed object can show problems well under that count.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a filter built against a standard-index field is generally treated as selective if it targets no more than about ________ percent of the first million records in the object.
questions.explain: Lesson 4 gives the standard-index selectivity threshold as roughly 30% of the first million targeted records (and roughly 15% beyond that), a looser bar than the custom-index threshold.

questions.prompt: Why is a custom index's selectivity threshold (roughly 10% of the first million records) stricter than a standard index's (roughly 30%)?
options: Custom indexes are a documented Salesforce design choice that requires a narrower, more selective filter before the optimizer will use them
Custom indexes don't actually affect query performance at all
There is no real difference between the two thresholds in practice
Custom indexes always cost more in API calls than standard indexes
questions.explain: Lesson 4 explains that Salesforce's published guidance simply holds custom indexes to a stricter selectivity bar than standard indexes, which is why a filter that clears the standard-index threshold might still fail the custom-index threshold on a different field.

questions.prompt: Select every filter pattern that Lesson 4 identifies as unselective, even when applied to an indexed field.
options: A negative operator such as != or NOT LIKE
A null check such as Field__c = null
A leading wildcard in a LIKE condition, such as LIKE '%smith%'
A simple equality condition on an indexed picklist field with a rare value
A range condition on an indexed date field
questions.explain: Negative operators, null checks, and leading-wildcard LIKE conditions are all called out as unselective regardless of indexing, because the optimizer can't use an index to evaluate them efficiently. A plain equality condition on a genuinely rare value, or a range condition on a date field, can both be selective.

questions.prompt: A dashboard's filter is already selective and backed by a standard index, but the query is still slow because it needs both a standard field and a custom field together on a 7-million-record object. Which Chapter 1 tool most directly addresses this specific bottleneck?
options: A skinny table, since it combines frequently-used standard and custom fields into one structure, avoiding the join that's otherwise required
A custom index on the same field that's already indexed
Switching the object's Organization-Wide Default to Private
Disabling the Recycle Bin for that object
questions.explain: Lesson 5 is explicit that the standard/custom field join, not the filter's selectivity, is what a skinny table specifically addresses — a problem that persists even after indexing and selectivity are both already correct.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 term to what it actually is.
right: An org-level partition (e.g., by region) used to pre-scope searches, reports, and SOQL/SOSL before other filtering
An ordered lookup structure letting the query engine find matching rows without scanning the whole object
A Salesforce-managed table combining frequently-used standard and custom fields, avoiding the standard/custom join
How small a fraction of an object's rows a filter condition is estimated to match
questions.explain: An index is the lookup structure itself; selectivity is how narrow a filter's matched fraction is; a skinny table avoids the standard/custom join; a division is an org-level partition used to pre-scope an entire object before other filtering runs.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 6 describe enabling divisions as a one-way architectural decision?
options: Because divisions cannot be disabled once enabled, and they're provisioned by Salesforce Support rather than through a self-service Setup option
Because divisions automatically delete all existing records once turned on
Because divisions can be freely toggled on and off at any time without consequence
Because divisions replace the org's entire sharing model permanently
questions.explain: Divisions cannot be disabled once enabled, which is exactly why Lesson 6 frames recommending them as a decision an architect has to be confident in going in, not something to try experimentally.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Trailhead's commonly cited guideline treats roughly ________ child records under one parent (or owned by one user) as the point where skew-related problems tend to start showing up.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 cites roughly 10,000 as Trailhead's commonly used guideline for ownership and parent skew — a planning threshold, not a hard platform-enforced limit.

questions.prompt: A single integration user ends up owning 300,000 of an object's 900,000 total records, with no single Account overloaded. What type of skew is this, per Lesson 7?
options: Lookup skew
Parent (account) skew
Ownership skew
This isn't a form of skew, since no Account is involved
questions.explain: Ownership skew happens when one user or queue owns a disproportionate share of an object's records, regardless of whether any single parent record is overloaded — exactly the scenario described.

questions.prompt: Why are Account and Opportunity specifically called out for parent (account) skew, more so than an arbitrary custom object?
options: Because they are the only two objects that support lookup relationships
Because their private sharing model requires briefly locking the parent record for certain child-record operations, which creates lock contention when too many children accumulate under one parent
Because Account and Opportunity records cannot be queried with SOQL
Because they are automatically stored in skinny tables regardless of configuration
questions.explain: Lesson 7 and Lesson 8 connect parent skew to a real mechanism: certain operations on child records briefly lock the parent under Account/Opportunity's private sharing model, and too many children under one parent multiplies how often concurrent transactions collide on that lock.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Bulk API's parallel and serial processing modes, per Lesson 9.
options: Parallel mode is the default because it maximizes throughput
Concurrency mode (parallel vs. serial) is set at the job level, so switching to serial means creating a separate job
Grouping a load's batches by parent ID is a recommended fix to try before switching to serial mode
Serial mode should be the first choice for any load, regardless of whether lock errors have occurred
Creating users and updating role hierarchies are operations Salesforce names as likely needing serial mode from the start
questions.explain: Parallel mode is the default for throughput; concurrency mode is job-level; grouping batches by parent ID is the recommended first fix; and user creation, ownership updates under private sharing, role updates, and territory updates are named as likely needing serial mode from the start. Serial mode is explicitly NOT the recommended starting point for every load.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of using deferred sharing calculation for a large structural change in the correct order, per Lesson 10.
items: Suspend automatic sharing calculation before making any structural changes
Make the full batch of structural changes (org-wide defaults, groups, queues, sharing rules, role moves)
Resume sharing calculation so it runs once, in bulk, across the whole batch
Allow insert/update-triggered automation to resume running normally
questions.explain: Lesson 10's documented sequence is to defer calculation first, make the complete batch of structural changes without recalculating after each step, resume calculation once so it runs in bulk, and only then let ordinary insert/update automation resume so validation and enrichment behave correctly afterward.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between archiving and deletion, per Lesson 11?
options: Deletion permanently removes data no longer needed at all; archiving moves data out of the active working set while still preserving it for potential future retrieval
They are two different names for exactly the same operation
Archiving only applies to custom objects, while deletion only applies to standard objects
Archiving always happens automatically on a fixed schedule, while deletion always requires a Support case
questions.explain: Archiving preserves a record's retrievability while removing it from the actively-queried working set; deletion permanently removes data the organization has decided it no longer needs at all.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D assumes a fixed mechanical split (archiving automatic, deletion Support-gated) that the lesson never states — both archiving and deletion can be manual, planned processes, and the real distinction is about whether the data's retrievability is preserved, not about who or what triggers the process.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce's documented retention window for a soft-deleted record sitting in the Recycle Bin is ________ days before it's scheduled for permanent removal.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 states the Recycle Bin's documented retention window as 15 days, after which a soft-deleted record is scheduled for permanent (hard) deletion.

questions.prompt: What problem does PK chunking solve, per Lesson 11, that ordinary field-value-based chunking doesn't handle well?
options: At very large scale (hundreds of millions of records), filtering by field value stops being a practical primary chunking strategy, so PK chunking splits the extract by record Id instead
PK chunking automatically deletes records as they're extracted
PK chunking removes the need for any backup step before deletion
PK chunking only works on Big Objects, never on standard or custom objects
questions.explain: PK chunking is a technique for combating slow performance on very large-scale extracts by chunking on the record's primary key (Id) rather than a business field, once field-value-based chunking stops scaling well.

questions.prompt: Match each Big Object constraint from Lesson 12 to what it actually limits.
right: Capped — there's a limit on how many Big Objects can be defined in one org
Restricted to a narrower set than standard/custom objects, commonly DateTime, Lookup, Number, Text, and Long Text Area
Not supported at all — an archiving pipeline needs an insert-only or explicitly-sequenced approach instead
Much more limited than standard/custom objects, appropriate since Big Objects hold settled historical data
questions.explain: Big Object field types are limited to a narrower supported set; upsert isn't supported at all; trigger/Flow automation support is much more restricted; and there's a per-org cap on how many Big Objects can be defined — all real constraints to design around before committing to a Big Object as an archive target.

questions.prompt: At roughly what volume does Salesforce's own guidance recommend hard delete through Bulk API 2.0, per Lesson 13?
options: Only when deleting fewer than 1,000 records
On the order of a million or more records
Hard delete is never recommended at any volume
Only on sandbox orgs, never production
questions.explain: Lesson 13 cites Salesforce's guidance that hard delete through Bulk API 2.0 is the recommended approach once a deletion operation reaches roughly a million or more records, since the alternative means carrying a large, costly Recycle Bin backlog.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about truncation, per Lesson 13.
options: Truncation clears an entire custom object at once, rather than deleting a filtered set of records
Truncation requires help from Salesforce Customer Support to execute
Truncation can be performed even if the org has already reached its limit on allowed custom objects
Truncation is mainly used to clear sandbox test data rather than as a general production deletion strategy
Truncation is available for standard objects like Account and Opportunity
questions.explain: Truncation clears an entire custom object at once, needs Support assistance, and is mainly a sandbox-oriented tool for clearing test data. It cannot be performed if the org has already reached its custom-object limit, and it applies to custom objects, not standard objects like Account or Opportunity.

questions.prompt: In the Meridian Logistics case study (Lesson 15), a monthly billing batch job consistently fails lock errors on the same handful of large national accounts. Which mechanism is this, and what's the recommended first fix?
options: Parent (account) skew causing lock contention; the first fix is reorganizing the job's batches to group by AccountId before considering serial mode
A missing custom index on Status__c; the first fix is requesting one from Salesforce Support
Sharing recalculation cost; the first fix is deferred sharing calculation
A leading-wildcard LIKE filter; the first fix is rewriting the query's WHERE clause
questions.explain: Lock failures consistently concentrated on the same handful of large accounts is the signature of parent skew, and the recommended first fix (per Lesson 9's guidance, applied in the case study) is reorganizing batches to group by AccountId before escalating to serial mode.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 15's sequenced remediation plan, put these steps in the recommended order for an org with multiple interacting LDV symptoms and no existing archiving process.
items: Establish an archiving process to shrink the active working set carrying years of unneeded historical data
Apply the batch-reorganization fix to the write-path problem and confirm it against the now-smaller active data set
Re-evaluate whether a custom index or skinny table is still needed once the active record count has dropped
Re-plan any future large structural sharing changes using deferred sharing calculation
questions.explain: Lesson 15's recommended sequence shrinks the active data set first, since that makes every other fix more effective (and sometimes unnecessary at the reduced scale), before re-applying the more targeted write-path and read-path fixes, with deferred sharing calculation planned in for future structural changes regardless.
